title: Universal school meals can convert stigma-free access into participation and learning gains while leaving food quality, waste, and household spillovers contested
source_unit: New York City Public Schools administrative meal system, New York City Comptroller review, and longitudinal student-level evaluation of universal free meals
geography: New York City public schools; citywide meal operations and middle-school evaluation

denominator.unit: longitudinal student-level evaluation of NYC middle schools adopting universal free lunch

lunch_participation_nonpoor.unit: percentage-point increase in school-lunch participation among students not previously eligible for free or reduced-price meals

lunch_participation_poor.unit: percentage-point increase among students previously eligible for free or reduced-price meals

math_effect_nonpoor.unit: standard deviations estimated math test-score increase among non-poor students

ela_effect_nonpoor.unit: standard deviations estimated English Language Arts test-score increase among non-poor students

mechanism.value: Universalizing a previously means-tested resource can reduce stigma and administrative sorting while increasing meal use and measured academic outcomes

observations.method: Difference-in-differences evaluation using longitudinal student-level New York City middle-school data, with additional instrumental-variable analysis of meal participation.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates concern historical middle schools and the study design; they do not establish current citywide effects, household food security, health, attendance, or durable cultural belonging.
observations.subgroup: Students previously eligible versus not previously eligible for subsidized meals in evaluated middle schools.
observations.counterinterpretation: The policy may operate through several channels—food access, stigma reduction, time, school routines, or selection into participating schools—and the study cannot turn the estimated score change into a universal welfare measure.

denominator.unit: school buildings in which NYC school food was served

meals_served.unit: meals served in FY2025 across participating NYC school-food buildings

daily_average.unit: meals served per day on average in FY2025

food_budget.unit: million US dollars spent on food within a 4.9 billion dollar NYC Public Schools operating budget

mechanism.value: Universal access has become a large public food and care infrastructure, not merely a targeted benefit; scale creates both reach and operational accountability obligations

observations.method: NYC Comptroller review using NYC Public Schools information and FY2025 meal-service data.
observations.uncertainty: Meals served are not unique students, consumed meals, nutritional adequacy, or a household-level estimate of food insecurity or grocery savings.
observations.subgroup: District, charter, non-public, and specialized school settings included in the reported service totals; the review does not provide a common individual denominator for all meals.
observations.counterinterpretation: High volume can coexist with uneven take-up, menu dissatisfaction, missed meals, food waste, or unequal access by schedule, disability, language, school location, or cultural and religious preference.

observations.period: 2025-2026 school year; public access and feedback route

denominator.unit: NYC Public Schools universal school-meals policy

eligibility.value: Breakfast, lunch, and afterschool meals are offered at no cost to all NYC Public Schools students during the school year

feedback.value: NYC Public Schools solicits family and student input through food-service surveys, menus, school contacts, and community meetings

mechanism.value: Formal universality removes an eligibility gate, but practical legitimacy still depends on whether meals are reachable, acceptable, culturally legible, and responsive to user feedback

observations.method: NYC Public Schools public program guidance and food-service feedback materials.
observations.uncertainty: The public guidance establishes availability and feedback channels, not response rates, menu changes attributable to feedback, consumption, or student trust.
observations.subgroup: All NYC Public Schools students during the school year, with menu and accommodation variation by school and program.
observations.counterinterpretation: A nominally universal program can still be uneven in practice because of timing, queueing, cafeteria conditions, accessibility, dietary needs, stigma residues, or family awareness.

observations.period: FY2025; operational compliance and waste surface

denominator.unit: food-providing programs reported in NYC's 2025 food-standards compliance table

annual_meals_all_reported_programs.unit: meals and snacks served annually across reporting programs in the compliance table

food_share_tables.unit: school buildings with food-share tables out of 1675 buildings where school food was served, according to the Comptroller review

mechanism.value: Public provision creates a second accountability problem after access: quality standards, surplus handling, waste, and operational feedback shape whether universal care becomes trusted everyday infrastructure

observations.method: NYC food-policy compliance reporting and Comptroller review of school food donation and composting operations.
observations.uncertainty: Compliance and food-sharing counts do not measure meal quality as experienced by students, actual waste avoided, food insecurity reduction, or educational outcomes.
observations.subgroup: School buildings and food programs rather than students or households; operational coverage varies across participating sites.
observations.counterinterpretation: Waste-management infrastructure can improve environmental performance without changing student take-up, and high meal volume can increase waste if menus or service conditions are poorly matched.

observations.period: FY2025 / 2024-2025 school year; current city performance and cultural-fit indicators

denominator.unit: NYC Public Schools Office of Food and Nutrition Services performance surface

student_satisfaction.unit: percent of students indicating satisfaction with Office of Food and Nutrition Services

mechanism.value: A universal meal system's practical legitimacy is observable through use volume, reported student satisfaction, and the availability of culturally or religiously responsive meal certification, while the public indicator remains aggregate

observations.method: NYC Mayor's Management Report FY2025 / Office of Food and Nutrition Services performance indicators sourced from NYC Public Schools and NYC School Survey results.
observations.uncertainty: Satisfaction is an aggregate survey indicator, not a causal measure of meal quality or a representative student-level outcome; meal counts are served meals rather than unique students or consumed meals; certification counts do not establish actual availability, uptake, or adequacy for every student needing halal or kosher options.
observations.subgroup: NYC public-school students and participating school buildings covered by the city performance indicators; subgroup breakdowns by income, race, disability, language, school, and dietary need are not supplied here.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher satisfaction can coexist with missed meals, food waste, queueing, culturally mismatched menus, or household food insecurity; certification capacity can coexist with uneven day-to-day access.

related_sources.claim: Current NYC Public Schools guidance describes free school-year meals and routes for menu and community feedback.
Earlier NYC policy analysis documents the administrative and participation logic behind universal school meals.

boundary: This record follows New York City's universal school-meals route from historical student-level evaluation through current program scale, access guidance, feedback channels, and operational compliance. It does not establish current causal effects, household food-security change, nutritional adequacy, equal practical access, or durable student trust and belonging across the city.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The Syracuse evaluation, NYC Comptroller review, NYC Public Schools guidance, and NYC food-policy compliance materials were reviewed for the reported historical effects, current scale, access rules, feedback channels, and waste/compliance boundaries.
